l: Lacedaemonian garrison, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: The Lacedaemonian garrison, fifteen hundred men in the Cadmea, initially repelled besiegers but, lacking provisions and relief, surrendered when auxiliaries demanded it and was dismissed under articles.

l: Callias, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Callias, a Syracusan historian enriched by Agathocles, advanced by praising him beyond his merits as pious and righteous despite his violations.

l: Chios, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Chios joined the Athenian confederacy after defecting from Lacedaemonian rule, aided Theban fleet preparations, came under Thebes, and later defended against an Athenian siege with allies.

l: Byzantium, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Byzantium is a city repeatedly drawn into Greek wars and changing control. It joined the Athenian confederacy as an early defector from Lacedaemonian rule, later was asked to help Thebes prepare a fleet and docks, and was brought under Theban obedience by Epaminondas. Athenian generals planned to besiege it, while opposing fleets moved toward the Hellespont. Ruled tyrannically by Clearchus, it later faced Philip’s siege, aided Perinthus, and received support from Athens and other Greeks until Philip withdrew. Naval fighting occurred near it, and Antigonus obtained Byzantine transports for an attack.

l: Rhodes, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Rhodes is a maritime city, built in the form of a theatre, with Digma, temples of Bacchus and Esculapius, and statues of Ptolemy, Cassander, and Lysimachus. Its shape worsened a flood: water ran to lower parts, more than five hundred died, and citizens fled upward until a broken wall spared the city from total destruction. Politically, it joined the Athenian confederacy after defecting from Lacedaemonian rule, later revolted from Athens, and was brought under Theban obedience by Epaminondas. Wealthy, well governed, and sustained by trade with Egypt, it favored Ptolemy and resisted Demetrius when he demanded hostages and harbour access. Citizens, inhabitants, and foreigners defended its walls and harbour through prolonged attacks, aided by Ptolemy, Cassander, and Lysimachus. Peace left it under its own laws without a garrison; it then honored Ptolemy and rebuilt its theatre and walls more gloriously.

l: Athenian confederacy, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: The Athenian confederacy was a union of cities joined with Athens against the Lacedaemonians. It grew as cities defected, preserved members’ own laws, placed them under Athenian administration, and ultimately included seventy equally represented cities, strengthening Athens and attracting others.

l: general diet or senate, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: A council of representatives from allied cities, established by the Athenians, meets at Athens by common consent, with each city, great or small, sending one representative.

l: plague of Carthage, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: A severe plague swept away many Carthaginians, endangering sovereignty; Africans deserted, Sardinia revolted, disorder spread, until Carthaginians recovered and subdued opponents.

l: Chabrias, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Chabrias is an Athenian general and commander of mercenary, land, and naval forces. He served Acoris without Athenian consent until recalled, then led Athenian forces in Euboea, defeated Pollis at Naxos, and helped protect Thebes by ordering mercenaries to stand firm against Agesilaus. He rescued Abdera from the Triballians and strengthened it with a garrison, defended Corinth against the Boeotians, and commanded at Chios. The records give differing endings: assassination after Abdera, or death defending his pierced ship at Chios.

l: Pharnabazus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Pharnabazus is a commander-in-chief appointed by the Persian king. He prepares money and war plans, requests Iphicrates from Athens, and commands the Persian army in the expedition against Egypt. After delaying the expedition for years, he disputes with Iphicrates over attacking Memphis and quarrels with him again after the army returns to Asia. Later, having revolted from the Persian king, he and Chares rout the king's troops despite a small force, and he funds Chares's soldiers.

l: Iphicrates, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Iphicrates, an Athenian general commanding Greek mercenaries, led forces in Persian and Egyptian expeditions. After urging an unsuccessful attack on Memphis, he secretly returned to Athens and became admiral. Later, equal commander against rebellious confederates, he refused battle in a storm, was accused of treason, fined, and dismissed.

l: Piraeus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Piraeus is a port at and of Athens. It is repeatedly contested in warfare: Sphodrias’s planned nighttime attack fails when Athenians detect it; Nicanor secretly seizes its walls and harbor mouth, and Alexander retains it rather than restoring it to Athens. Cassander later seizes it with ships and men, uses it as a return point, and holds it through his forces. Finally Demetrius assaults it, gains entry with help from insiders, and captures it from Cassander’s garrison.

l: Timotheus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Timotheus, son of Clearchus, is portrayed as a commander appointed for an expedition against the Lacedaemonians. As admiral of the Athenian fleet, he blockades a city in Cephallenia, seeks Acarnanian support, allies with Acetas, king of the Molussians, and defeats the Spartans at Leucades. He receives Zacynthian exiles, helps them seize Arcadia, is redirected between Corcyra and Thrace, and is restored after Athens removes him. Later, sharing command against rebellious confederates, he refuses battle in a storm; Chares charges treason, and Athens fines and dismisses him. He is also accused of devising a killing scheme and concealing further deaths.

l: Euboea, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Euboea, containing Chalcis, saw most chief cities except Acta join an association with Athens, prompting Athenian forces to secure allies and suppress opponents. Internal factions, backed by Boeotians and Athenians, then fought a devastating civil war and made peace. Later Ptolemy’s and Cassander’s armies confronted there; Cassander left Plistarchus guarding Chalcis and marched away.

l: Jason of Pherae, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Jason of Pherae, a prince skilled in military affairs, aided the Thebans and urged peace amid uncertain war. He later pressed the Thessalians to seek Greek sovereignty, allied with Amyntas of Macedonia, and was assassinated by seven young men or Polydorus.

l: Peparethos, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Peparethos was besieged by Alexander of Pherae. An Athenian garrison under Leosthenes relieved the city, but Alexander later captured one Peparethian galley and six hundred prisoners during his victory at Panormus.

l: Elians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Elians rejected a forced unlawful Olympiad, executed oracle-robbing mercenaries, regained liberty and recovered the temple at Olympus, then expelled Arcadians from Lassia but were defeated and contested the Olympic games.

l: Corinthians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Corinthians inhabit Corinth and, when Syracuse suffers internal conflict and seeks liberty, judge assistance just, decree Timoleon’s mission, and prepare forces and arms for aid.

l: Phocians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: The Phocians were a Greek people in the Phocian war. Condemned by the Amphictyons for cultivating oracle-claimed land at Cirrha, they made Philomelus their absolute general; he asserted their ancestral claim to the Oracle at Delphos and enlisted a thousand Peltastates. They supported Philomelus and Onomarchus in fighting over Apollo's temple and sacred treasures, seizing and robbing the oracle and using sacred wealth from Delphi to fund war. Allied with Athenians and aided by mercenaries and outside support, they won some engagements but repeatedly suffered defeats against the Boeotians and Philip of Macedon. After Onomarchus was killed, Phayllus rebuilt their forces, but later losses continued under Phalaecus. When Phalaecus departed, they surrendered to Philip and received severe Amphictyonic penalties, losing temple access and Council membership.

l: Thrace, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Thrace is a kingdom and region bordering the Macedonians, valued for places such as advantageously situated Amphipolis. Philip conquered it before an alliance formed. It suffered Triballian incursions, fighting between Triballians and Abderites, Memnon’s rebellion, and an insurrection; Antipater campaigned there. Diegylis ruled violently, then Seuthes ruled during Lysimachus’s invasion.

l: Pollis, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: A Lacedaemonian admiral, Pollis commands sixty-five warships at Naxos, kills Cedon and defeats part of the Athenian left, before Chabrias defeats his fleet.

l: Naxos, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Naxos was besieged by Chabrias and the Athenian fleet. Pollis came to its assistance, but the ensuing naval battle ended in an Athenian victory.

l: Sparta, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Sparta is a city, the capital of the Lacedaemonians. It protected Sphodrias before its senate after his attempt to seize the Piraeus, then reorganized its forces and policy toward remaining confederates. Answering supporters in Corcyra, it ordered Alcidas there and sent Mnasippus's fleet to seize the island. Fearing Theban loss of its sovereign command of Greece, it suffered defeat at Leuctra and lost its principality; chief nobles were received by Antipater as hostages. During Epaminondas's invasion, Sparta was besieged and repeatedly threatened or attacked. Agis warned it, Agesilaus organized defense, Dionysius supplied Gauls and Spaniards, and its defenders resisted until the attackers withdrew.

l: Athenian–Spartan peace, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: is_between Lacedaemonians [and Athenians; continued until this time] The Lacedaemonians and Athenians had maintained peace for several years. The peace ended after Sphodrias attempted to seize the Piraeus and Sparta failed to punish him.

l: Battle of Naxos, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Naval battle near Naxos and Paros, where Chabrias led eighty-three Athenian ships against Pollis’s sixty-five Lacedaemonian ships; Athens won, capturing eight ships and crews.

l: Peloponnesian War, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: precedes Battle of Naxos [the first Athenian naval victory since the war] The Battle of Naxos was described as the first naval victory gained by the Athenians since the Peloponnesian War. The text contrasts it with Cnidus, where Athenian success depended on the Persian king's assistance.

l: Spartan army, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: The Spartan army, commanded by Agesilaus and including Sciritae, was reorganized into ten divisions with valued troop types, then entered Boeotia with more than eighteen thousand foot and fifteen hundred horse.

l: Athenian fleet, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: The Athenian fleet escorted ships carrying grain to the Piraeus and later sailed to Naxos under Chabrias. It numbered eighty-three ships and defeated the Lacedaemonian fleet. The Athenian fleet was expanded for the war and eventually sailed to Corcyra under Timotheus and Iphicrates. It arrived too late to decide the main struggle but captured nine ships sent from Sicily to aid the Lacedaemonians.

l: the Triballians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: The Triballians, a Thracian people, invaded neighboring territory during a corn scarcity with thirty thousand armed men, plundered the Abderites, suffered losses, then returned and nearly destroyed their army.

l: Abdera, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Abdera was attacked and plundered by the Triballians. Its forces first defeated more than two thousand invaders, but were later surrounded and nearly destroyed until Chabrias arrived.

l: the Abderites, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: The Abderites attacked the scattered Triballians and killed more than two thousand of them. After the Triballians returned, the Abderites fought with neighboring Thracians but were left exposed when those allies withdrew; Chabrias later delivered them and strengthened their city with a garrison.

l: Spartans, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: The Spartans held Orchomenos with a strong garrison but were routed by five hundred Thebans despite being twice as numerous. Timotheus also defeated them in a sea-fight at Leucades. The Spartans feared that the growing power of the Thebans would threaten their supremacy and prepared to make war against them. They were defeated by the Thebans at Leuctra and lost their principality, according to a prophecy cited in the account.

l: Orchomenos, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: is_garrisoned_by the Spartans [with a strong garrison] Orchomenos was held by the Spartans with a strong garrison. The Thebans attacked it, and the Spartan force was routed in a sharp encounter.

l: Egyptians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: The Egyptians are a rebellious people against the Persians, repeatedly organizing Egypt’s defense. They garrison Pelusium, fortify the Nile mouths, strengthen Memphis, and prepare for invasion; after resisting and exploiting Persian failures, they eventually force the Persians from Egypt. Under Nectanebus, they fight Persia and aid Sidon with Greek mercenaries, but defeats, disputes with auxiliaries, urban seditions, and an attempted surrender at Bubastis weaken them. Led by Nectanabis after Tachos flees, they besiege and pursue Tachos and Agesilaus, yet lose despite superior numbers. Seeking an end to troubles, they expel foreigners; displaced people depart or settle in Judea. Later, they condemn Ptolemy’s cruelty and excesses.

l: the general peace, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: The general peace, concluded by Greece, requires self-government and garrison withdrawals; commissioners enforce it, but the Thebans resist by claiming Boeotia as subject.

l: Epaminondas, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Epaminondas is a Theban philosopher and military commander, esteemed by his people and praised among the Grecians for learning, courage, justice, patience, frugality, contempt for wealth, and freedom from covetousness. He studied the liberal sciences, especially Pythagorean philosophy, learning from Lysis. After arguing for the Thebans before the common Greek assembly against a peace decree, he was appointed general and entrusted with the whole war. Against the Lacedaemonians he used an oblique phalanx, concentrating his strongest soldiers on his own wing, and helped win at Leuctra. He then led Boeotian and allied campaigns in the Peloponnesus and Laconia, withdrew from a costly attack on Sparta, urged the rebuilding of Messene, and fought near Corinth. Though once demoted to private soldier on suspicion of treason, he was chosen to lead a desperate retreat from Thessaly, protected the army with light troops and cavalry, repulsed Alexander’s forces, and brought it safely off. He advocated Theban dominion of the sea and brought Rhodes, Chios, and Byzantium into Theban obedience. Finally, commanding against Mantinea, he charged the Lacedaemonians, killed their general, broke their division, received a mortal breast wound, and died after learning his side had won.

l: Peloponnesus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Peloponnesus is a place containing Sicyon, Corinth, the battle of Mantinea, and Greek cities of Sicily. It is marked first by severe internal disorder after democratic governments were restored: exiles, conspiracies, punishments, tumults, and seditions affected Phialia, Corinth, Megara, and Sicyon. Extraordinary earthquakes and inundations then destroyed cities and killed many, especially at Helice and Bura in Achaia. It became a theater of invasion and war as Boeotians, Phocians, Locrians, Arcadians, Argives, and Elians entered, and Epaminondas broke through Corinth’s defenses. Peace after Mantinea quickly failed over towns incorporated into Megalopolis. Later it hosted discharged soldiers near Taenarus and communities joining the Greek confederacy. Successive struggles brought Polyperchon, Cassander, Alexander, Aristodemus, Antigonus, Ptolemy’s commanders, and Telesphorus: cities and garrisons changed hands, Cassander controlled Argos and most of Messenia, and Telesphorus freed Alexander’s garrisons except at Sicyon and Corinth.

l: Argos, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: has Argive democracy [as its form of government] Argos was governed by a democracy when violent conflict arose between popular leaders and the city's great men. More than sixteen hundred prominent men and the orators who had inflamed the people were killed.

l: Corinth, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Corinth was a city in Achaia, between Cenchreae and Lechaeum. Alethes enlarged it and ruled for thirty-eight years; after its royal succession ended, the Bacchidae jointly governed, annually appointing a Prytanis, until Cypselus. It later faced war with the Lacedaemonians, sedition, and assaults by Epaminondas; Chabrias and the Athenians defended it, driving out Boeotians who entered its gates. It aided Sicilian affairs: Dion gathered mercenaries and arms there, and Corinth sent Timoleon to aid the Syracusans. It hosted Alexander’s meeting with Greek representatives, where he became general of all Greece. Contested by Ptolemy, Cassander, and Demetrius, it was captured by Demetrius, who took its havens, Sisyphium, and citadel, restored liberty, and garrisoned the citadel. Romans later destroyed it; almost a hundred years afterward, Caius Julius Caesar undertook its rebuilding.

l: Sicyon, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Sicyon, ruled by Epopeus, passed from Cratesipolis to Ptolemy, who garrisoned it. Demetrius then captured it by night; its garrison withdrew to the castle and surrendered. He moved inhabitants there, leveled the harbor-side city, aided rebuilding, and renamed it Demetriades. It executes innovators only after full conviction.

l: the incursions into Thrace, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: targets the Abderites [for provisions] The incursions into Thrace began when the Triballians, short of corn, entered the territories of the Abderites with thirty thousand armed men. The first incursion ended with heavy Triballian losses, while the second resulted in the near-destruction of the Abderite forces before Chabrias intervened.

l: the battle at Orchomenos, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: The battle at Orchomenos occurred when five hundred Thebans engaged the Spartan garrison that had sallied from the city. The Thebans routed the Spartans even though the latter were twice as numerous.

l: the Peloponnesian seditions, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: involves Peloponnesus [with banishments and confiscations] The Peloponnesian seditions followed the restoration of democratic governments and involved banishments, confiscations, conspiracies, and killings. Phialian exiles seized Herea, attacked their city during the Bacchic festival, later raised mercenaries, and were eventually defeated and driven to Argos.

l: Bacchus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Bacchus is a terrestrial god honored at Alexander’s victorious feast and sacred day. Said to have conquered the Indians and founded Nysa, he is revered by the Nysaeans; Alexander sacrifices to him, while priests blame neglected worship for misfortunes.

l: Egyptian revolt, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: is_a revolt [against Persian rule] The revolt of the Egyptians prompted the king of Persia to send a major army and fleet against Egypt.

l: Persian army, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: numbers two hundred thousand barbarians [mustered at Acest in Syria] The Persian army included two hundred thousand barbarians, twenty thousand Greeks, three hundred three-banked galleys, two hundred smaller ships, and many transports. It fought at Mendesium but withdrew when Egyptian resistance and the Nile flood made further operations impracticable.

l: Greek mercenaries, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: numbers twenty thousand [under Iphicrates] Twenty thousand Greek mercenaries served under Iphicrates in the Persian expedition against Egypt.

l: Syria, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Syria is a kingdom and region repeatedly contested and brought low. Antipater assigned it to Laomedon of Mitylene, but Ptolemy captured Laomedon and took all Syria. Antigonus entered Upper Syria, faced demands to yield it to Ptolemy, later recovered it after Ptolemy withdrew, and returned there after abandoning Egypt. After the Romans conquered Perseus, Syria endured disturbances from rival royal plots and popular changes of rulers.

l: Egyptian army, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: defends Egypt [against the Persian invasion] The Egyptian army defended the river entrances, relieved the fort at Mendesium, and later attacked the Persian forces repeatedly until they became increasingly strong.

l: Nectanabis, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Nectanabis, king of Egypt and commander of its forces, relied on difficult entrances and natural defenses, fortifying Pelusium and guarding Nile crossings. Tachos's son, he joined a revolt against his father, won commanders and soldiers with gifts and promises, took Egypt, then led over one hundred thousand men against Tachos and was defeated by Agesilaus.

l: Nile, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: The Nile flows through Egypt. Its seven mouths, forts, bridges, height, and guarded waters made entry and military movement difficult. Overflowing waters ruined works and obstructed crossings; current, shifting sand, crocodiles, and capture caused severe losses. Its guarded mouths and river-boats ultimately blocked land forces and limited fleet operations.

l: Pelusium, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Pelusium was a strongly fortified Egyptian frontier city toward Syria at the first mouth of the Nile, defended by trench, walls, blocked waterways, obstacles, and five thousand men under Philophron. Lacrates besieged it, drained the trench, breached the walls, and it surrendered after Nectanebus left for Memphis, receiving a Persian garrison.

l: Memphis, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Memphis was described as the most important Egyptian garrison. Iphicrates urged that it be attacked before the Egyptian army assembled, but Pharnabazus refused.

l: Conon, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: is_made_admiral_of Persian fleet [the Persian fleet] Conon was made admiral of the Persian fleet. He commanded it in the sea-fight at Cnidus, where Pisander and the Lacedaemonian fleet were defeated.

l: Iphicratean military reforms, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: changes soldiers' shoes [to make them easier to put on, march in, and remove] Iphicrates replaced heavy shields with moderately sized targets, lengthened the spears and swords, and altered the soldiers' shoes. The lighter equipment produced the class called peltasts, or targeteers, and was praised through experience.

l: oligarchy, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Oligarchies governed some Greek cities under the influence of Antipater's friends and favorites. Polyperchon and his allies resolved to abolish oligarchy throughout the cities of Greece. Those who favored the oligarchy were condemned after the Athenians restored magistrates who favored democracy. Some were sentenced to death, while others were banished and had their goods confiscated.

l: Zacynthus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: The inhabitants of Zacynthus expelled their magistrates and sought help from Athens and the Lacedaemonians. The island became a scene of conflict between its townsmen and exiles supported by Timotheus.

l: Zacynthian exiles, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: occupy Arcadia [a strong castle on Zacynthus] The expelled magistrates of Zacynthus fled to Timotheus, joined his fleet, and returned to the island. With his assistance they seized the strong castle of Arcadia and harassed the townsmen.

l: Arcadia, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: It was invaded by Lacedaemonian forces under Polytropus, whose army was defeated at Orchomenus. It later served as the base for the allied forces that invaded Laconia and returned there after ravaging the country.

l: Corcyra, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Corcyra is an island important for control of the sea. Threatened by Lacedaemonians and supporters, its inhabitants resisted; Ctesias strengthened defenses, defeated the enemy, and helped nearly end the war. Cleonymus then captured it, took treasure, garrisoned it, and returned with forces after reverses in Italy.

l: Ctesias, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: commands Athenian fleet [sent to relieve Corcyra] Ctesias entered Corcyra secretly at night with five hundred men. He reconciled the divided townsmen, organized the defense, killed two hundred enemies in a sortie, and later killed Mnasippus and many of his troops in battle.

l: Plataea, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: is_razed_by Thebans [after its inhabitants surrendered] Plataea allied with Athens and sought an Athenian garrison. The Thebans invaded, expelled the inhabitants, razed the city, and forced the Plataeans to settle in Athens.

l: Mnasippus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: commands Lacedemonian fleet [against Corcyra] Mnasippus led a Lacedemonian fleet and fifteen hundred men against Corcyra. He defeated the Corcyrians at first but was later killed by Ctesias in a sharp engagement.

l: Lacedemonian fleet, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: The Lacedemonian fleet sent Mnasippus to Corcyra with sixty-five ships and fifteen hundred men. It captured or drove off the Corcyrian ships and initially routed the defenders, but its campaign failed after Mnasippus was killed.

l: eunuch who murdered Evagoras, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: becomes_king_of Salamis [after murdering Evagoras] The eunuch treacherously murdered Evagoras and seized the kingship of Salamis for himself.

l: Romans, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: The Romans are a political and military people whose record centers on repeated war, expansion, alliances, public conduct, and changing character. It opens with conflict and diplomacy in Italy: they hold a league with the Samnites and a truce with the Praenestines, fight the Samnites, recover Sora, Harpina, and Serenia, and ultimately make peace after twenty-two years and six months. They then ally with the Marsi, Peligni, and Marrucini. Further accounts describe alternating successes and setbacks against the Samnites, including fighting at Ferentum and Saticula, defeat at Lautulae, colonies at Luceria and Pontia, captures, garrisons, and eventual control of revolting cities. They also defend Sutrium, fight Etruscans, and relieve the Iapyges. Their wars broaden into Sicily, Africa, and beyond. They intervene at Messana, take Agrigentum and Panormus, besiege Lilybaeum, and endure defeats, storms, shipwreck near Camarina, disease, shortages, and naval losses before making peace with the Carthaginians after twenty-four years. They fight the Lusitanians, suffer greatly under Viriathus, and later regain power in a long war with the Italians. Internal conflict then raises Sylla, Julius Caesar, and Augustus. The records repeatedly assess Roman values. They are praised for public-spirited mutual commendation, piety, patience, constancy, justice in war, observance of leagues and oaths, and clemency toward conquered peoples. After conquering Perseus and Macedonia, they proclaim liberty, preserve laws, and reduce tribute. Yet they are also portrayed as conquerors who become severe, destroying Corinth, Carthage, Numantia, and the kingdom of Macedonia, and as changing from frugal moderation into luxury and insatiable desire for riches. They judge Sylla worthy of the consulship, address the exile of Metellus, impose terms on Antiochus, and close with the taking of Veii, defeat and recovery after the Gauls captured Rome, and Marcus Furius's relief of the city.

l: earthquakes and inundations in Peloponnesus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Nighttime earthquakes destroyed Helice and Bura as buildings collapsed; the sea later swept away people and houses, attributed to nature or divine anger.

l: Achaia, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Achaia was the region where Helice and Bura were destroyed or greatly damaged by the earthquakes and inundations. Demetrius took Bata by assault, received the surrender of Scyros, and then freed the remaining cities of Achaia. The governors of the cities surrendered when Cassander and Polyperchon sent them no assistance and Demetrius approached with a powerful army and large engines.

l: Helice, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: is_in Achaia [formerly called Ionia] Helice, one of the principal cities of Achaia, was chiefly affected by the disaster. Its people were said to have angered Neptune by refusing the Ionians access to ancient religious images and by imprisoning their ambassadors.

l: Bura, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: is_in Achaia Bura, another city of Achaia, shared in the refusal to grant the Ionians the requested religious images and also suffered in the earthquakes and inundations.

l: Neptune, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: is_associated_with earthquakes and inundations in Peloponnesus [according to the religious explanation] Neptune was said to have punished Helice and Bura for violating religious rights. He was regarded as the god who controlled inundations and earthquakes and as the deity especially worshipped throughout Peloponnesus.

l: Ionians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: The Ionians moved their Panionion festival from Mycale because of wars and consulted Delphi about obtaining sacred images. After the people of Helice and Bura refused their request, the Ionians sacrificed at Neptune's altar under an Athenian public edict.

l: Ephesus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: has_garrison Demetrius's soldiers [garrison placed in the castle] Ephesus was recovered by Demetrius after he landed there and encamped before it. He restored it to its former obedience, allowed the garrison installed by Prepelaus to depart safely, and placed a strong garrison of his own in the castle.

l: Fabius, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Fabius is a general and historian of Roman affairs, credited with preserving the Roman commonwealth through valour and policy. In Etruria he raided higher Etruria, defeated Etruscans near Perusia, made peace with communities, captured Castula, and lifted Sutrium's siege. Appointed against Viriathus, he initially saw Viriathus decline, but Viriathus rallied and compelled him to accept dishonourable terms.

l: Fiery Beam comet, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: casts shadow upon the earth [even at noon] The Fiery Beam comet, named for its shape, appeared in the heavens for several nights and was said to be bright enough to cast a shadow on the earth by night. Its appearance was interpreted as a sign preceding the fall of Lacedaemonian sovereignty.

l: fall of Lacedaemonian sovereignty, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: The fall of Lacedaemonian sovereignty, foretold by the Fiery Beam comet, culminates in a great defeat that unexpectedly ends nearly five hundred years of rule over Greece.

l: Chaldeans, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Chaldeans, famous for astrology, predicted Alexander’s death after entering Babylon, sent Belephants to warn him, and urged avoidance and rebuilding Belus’s sepulchre, but he disregarded them.

l: Leuctra, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Leuctra is a battlefield where Lacedaemonians and Boeotians encamped and fought; its tombs shaped Epaminondas’s response to ominous signs before he and the Thebans defeated the Spartans there.

l: battle of Leuctra, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: The battle of Leuctra was a famous, decisive Theban and Boeotian victory under Epaminondas over the Lacedaemonians and Spartans. Epaminondas led the smaller Theban force in an oblique formation, killing about four thousand Lacedaemonians and about three hundred Boeotians. It destroyed much Lacedaemonian strength and encouraged the Thebans.

l: Hercules, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Hercules, a terrestrial god and ancient hero, failed to take Aornos, was restored to Alexander’s kingdom by Polyperchon, then murdered at Cassander’s urging.

l: Thessaly, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Thessaly is a region and province repeatedly contested by rulers and armies. It was associated with Jason’s growing power and ambition to lead it toward Greek sovereignty, while its forces supported the Thebans. Polydorus and then his brother Alexander ruled it tyrannically and oppressively; Alexander of Macedonia later promised to restore its cities but garrisoned and controlled them. It became the setting for Pelopidas’s imprisonment and release, Philip’s war with the Phocians, and major fighting involving Onomarchus, Leonatus, Antipater, Craterus, and Greek forces. Its cavalry shifted from Antipater to Leosthenes and the Athenians, and most Thessalians joined the Greek confederacy. The Aetolians recruited local support there before Polyperchon recovered the province. Finally, Demetrius entered through Larissa, captured or recovered places, and faced Cassander’s forces, whose soldiers later deserted to Antigonus.

l: Thessalians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: The Thessalians are a military and political group whose cavalry is repeatedly central to their actions. Jealous of Jason of Pherae's growing power, they nevertheless appoint him general of all their forces and entrust him with the war. They fight Alexander of Pherae, suffer losses, seek Theban aid under Pelopidas, and regain towns after Alexander's defeat. As Amphictyonic confederates, they first support Apollo's temple against the Phocians, are defeated at Argola, briefly remain neutral after Onomarchus's bribe, then join Philip, help defeat the Phocians, and take part in arrangements for the Pythian games. In the Lamian War, their cavalry defeats Leonatus's cavalry but cannot prevent defeat after Antipater attacks the infantry.

l: Phocis, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Phocis is a region repeatedly attacked and plundered by the Boeotians, leaving its people weakened. Defeated at the end of the Sacred War, it faced razing or conversion of its cities into villages and owed Delphi sixty talents annually until restitution was complete.

l: Scytalism, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Scytalism was the name given by the Greeks to the unprecedented slaughter during the Argive sedition. The name referred to the manner in which the killings were carried out with clubs.

l: Argive sedition, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Scytalism, the Argive sedition, began as popular leaders incited Argos against great men; accusations and executions killed suspected conspirators, then the violence consumed its orators before peace returned.

l: Lycomedes of Mantinea, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Lycomedes of Mantinea, Arcadian commander-in-chief, led forces to defeat Lacedaemonians near Orchomenus, then captured Pellene, killed its garrison, and returned before relief arrived.

l: Perdiccas, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Perdiccas is a Macedonian commander and protector of the kings who becomes the kingdom’s effective superintendent after receiving Alexander’s ring under Philip III. He commands Macedonians, Oresteans, Lyncestians, and the king’s army, possesses the king’s forces, and exercises executive power. Early in his rule he submits costly plans to a council, suppresses revolt through executions, including turbulent soldiers and Meleager, and sends Python against revolting Greeks. He pursues Pausanias with Leonatus and Attalus, conquers Ariarathes and Cappadocia with King Philip, executes Ariarathes, gives Cappadocia to Eumenes, restores Samos and its long-exiled people, and campaigns in Pisidia. His rule is marked by cruelty, ambition, and conflict. He marries Nicæa to preserve an alliance with Antipater, then Cleopatra while seeking the kingdom and sole monarchy. He targets Antigonos, suspects Ptolemy’s increasing power, and sends Eumenes with troops to hold the Hellespont against Antipater and Craterus. After Antigonos flees, Perdiccas leads the kings and army against Ptolemy in Egypt. There the Nile frustrates his works and a fort assault; a failed crossing kills more than two thousand soldiers, alienates the army, and prompts commanders and horsemen to kill him after three years of sovereign command. Later records describe him as dead, with Alcetas and Attalus among his remaining friends and kindred capable of opposing Antigonus. One record also describes a Perdiccas who deserts Eumenes and is captured and punished after Eumenes sends Phenices against him.

l: Philip, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Philip is a Macedonian king, ruler, general, and later supreme governor of Greece whose career moves from hostage to expansive monarch and then ends in assassination, though later records also attach a harsher, troubled reign to a Philip of Macedon. Held hostage by the Illyrians and sent to Thebes, he escaped and became king after Perdiccas was killed. He secured Macedonia by defeating Pæones, Illyrians, Thracians, and other opponents; captured places including Amphipolis, Pydna, Methone, Micaberna, Torone, Olynthus, and Elatea; enlarged his kingdom; and drew wealth from gold mines and tribute. His methods combine military force, mercenaries, bribery, and diplomacy: he said gold enlarged his dominion more than his sword, yet he also rewarded bravery and released Athenian prisoners without ransom. In Thessaly he removed tyrants, restored cities to liberty, and won enduring Thessalian alliance. He defended the oracle, participated in Amphictyonic decisions, and ended the Sacred War, actions linked to his growing authority. His ambition then widened to sovereignty over Greece and war against Persia. After making peace when resistance checked his sieges of Perinthus and Byzantium, he defeated Athenians and Boeotians at Chaeronea, renewed peace with Athens, garrisoned Thebes, and was chosen generalissimo of Greece with absolute power. He began the Persian war by sending Attalus and Parmenio into Asia, consulted the Delphic oracle, and arranged Cleopatra's marriage to Alexander, king of Epirus. He was stabbed and killed by Pausanias of Orestis at Aegae after about twenty-four years of rule; Alexander succeeded him. Other records praise him as Europe’s greatest and most victorious prince, crediting mild treatment of conquered people and a governmental order for Greek cities, while also describing a Philip influenced toward cruelty and tyranny, piracy, plunder, executions, unnecessary wars, defeat, and preservation through Roman clemency.

l: Polydorus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Polydorus, a Thessalian prince, was reportedly brother of Jason of Pherae and, while drunk, was poisoned to death by his brother Alexander the Pheraean.

l: sedition in Rome, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: causes anarchy in Rome [for some time] The sedition arose because some people supported making consuls while others supported creating military tribunes in their place. It led to anarchy for some time.

l: military tribunes, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Six military tribunes, including Caius Verginius, Servilius Sulpitius, Lucius Quintius, Caius Cornelius, and Caius Valerius, were chosen after Rome's anarchy.

l: Alexander of Pherae, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Alexander of Pherae became ruler of Thessaly after poisoning and succeeding his brother Polydorus. He reigned for eleven years as a tyrant, ruling with oppression and becoming hated by all men. After Alexander, king of Macedonia, captured Larissa and Cranon, he fled to Pherae. He imprisoned Pelopidas and Ismenias, massacred the people of Scotussa, besieged Peparethos, fought the Thessalians, and received Athenian assistance against the Thebans. Though he won repeated victories and initially held the advantage, he was forced into peace: he restored captured towns, ceded Magnesia and Phthiotis to the Boeotians, and was confined to Pherae. He was ultimately murdered by his Theban wife, with help from his brothers Lycophron and Tisiphonus.

l: Alexander, king of Macedonia, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Alexander, king of Macedonia, aided the Aleuadas against Alexander the Pheraean by joining deserters and bringing forces to Larissa, captured Larissa and Cranon, promised the Thessalians restoration, then garrisoned and retained their cities.

l: Larissa, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Larissa is a city with a citadel separate from it. Its Aleuadas sought Macedonian help against Alexander the Pheraean; citizens opened its gates to Alexander, king of Macedonia, who mastered the city and later seized the castle. Later it surrendered to Demetrius, who took the citadel, chained its garrison, and restored ancient laws and liberties.

l: Aleuadas, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: The Aleuadas were high-born people of Larissa who, fearing Alexander the Pheraean’s wickedness, conspired to dethrone him and sought help from Alexander, king of Macedonia.

l: conspiracy to dethrone Alexander the Pheraean, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: is_conducted_by Aleuadas The Aleuadas of Larissa formed a conspiracy to remove Alexander the Pheraean from power. They traveled to Macedonia and negotiated with Alexander, king of Macedonia, for military assistance.

l: cities of Thessaly, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Alexander, king of Macedonia, promised to restore the cities of Thessaly to the Thessalians after taking Larissa and Cranon. He did not keep his promise, instead placing garrisons in the cities and retaining them under his own control.

l: Boeotians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: The Boeotians are a people defined in these records by shifting alliances, wars, and military interventions. They first appear allied with the Phocians and Locrians under Epaminondas and Pelopidas, invading Laconia, helping rebuild Messene, and unsuccessfully attacking Corinth. They fought the Lacedemonians and their allies, endured attack and retreat in Thessaly, uncovered a conspiracy involving Orchomenian horsemen, and sent Pelopidas with seven thousand men to aid the Thessalians. Under Epaminondas they aided the Tegeans and defeated the Lacedaemonians at Mantinea, where he was mortally wounded; they also intervened in Euboea before returning home and disarming. Their central later conflict was the war against the Phocians. In support of the temple, oracle, and Amphictyonic decrees, they allied with Locrians and Amphictyons, raised armies, won several battles, invaded and plundered Phocis, but also suffered defeat at Coronea. Exhausted, they sought Philip's aid and supported him with the Thessalians at the war's end. They then joined Athens at Chaeronea after Demosthenes' appeal, suffered heavy losses, and made peace with Philip. After Thebes' destruction, they possessed its territory and opposed Athens, but were defeated near Phlitsa. Finally, after holding a garrison among the Chalcidians, fear of Demetrius led them to leave their league with Cassander.

l: Locrians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: The Locrians, a Greek people including the Epicnemidii, opposed Philomelus after he seized the temple. Defeated near Delphos and at the Rocks of Phaedra, they suffered invasion, losses, and prisoners, then sought Theban aid and joined the Boeotians against the Phocians.

l: Messenians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Messenians were a people repeatedly oppressed and expelled by the Lacedaemonians. Survivors settled at Naupactus, Cephalenia, and Sicily, where they founded Messana; others were invited by Epaminondas to repopulate Messene. Included in the general Greek league after Mantinea, they later received the Mamertines as allies, who massacred them and seized their city.

l: Orchomenus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: is_destroyed_by Thebans [the men were killed and women and children enslaved] Three hundred horsemen of Orchomenus joined Theban fugitives in a plan to change the government of Thebes. After the conspiracy was exposed, the city was captured and razed, its men were killed, and its women and children were sold as slaves.

l: Laconia, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: is_a country [ancient Spartan territory] The allied army invaded and devastated Laconia with fire and sword. The country had reportedly escaped such devastation for five hundred years before this invasion.

l: Messene, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: is_a Grecian city [repopulated and restored to its former grandeur] Messene had long been destroyed and left desolate by the Lacedaemonians. Epaminondas and his allies rebuilt it, repopulated it with returning Messenians and other settlers, and divided its territory among the inhabitants.

l: Messenia, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: is_ruled_by Lacedaemonians [before its restoration] Messenia was first associated with the family of Neleus and Nestor, then with Orestes and Cresphontes’s descendants, before coming under Lacedaemonian control. Its inhabitants later revolted under Aristomenes, were expelled after further wars, and eventually returned when Messene was rebuilt.

l: Messana, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Messana first resisted Agathocles and sheltered Syracusan exiles, but expelled them, admitted him, and served his purges. Foreign soldiers later murdered their hosts, married their wives, and seized it as the Mamertines. After Hiero’s victory nearly forced surrender, Hannibal allied with and reinforced them. Besieged by Hiero and Carthaginians after Roman intervention, it was relieved when Appius Claudius arrived and Hiero withdrew.

l: Epaminondas’s invasion of the Peloponnesus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: The invasion was undertaken after the Arcadians sought Theban assistance against Sparta. Led by Epaminondas and Pelopidas, the allied forces entered the Peloponnesus, invaded Laconia, threatened Sparta, and withdrew after ravaging the country. Epaminondas entered the Peloponnesus with all his forces, joined by the Achaians and other allies. He restored Dymon, Naupactus, and Calydon to their ancient liberties before making another expedition into Thessaly.

l: siege of Sparta, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: is_a military siege [conducted by Epaminondas's army] Epaminondas’s army approached Sparta and nearly took the city by storm. The defenders inflicted heavy losses from strong positions, and Epaminondas ordered a retreat.

l: rebuilding of Messene, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Epaminondas persuaded the Arcadians and other allies to rebuild Messene as a strategically placed city against Sparta. The city was repopulated, its land was distributed by lot, and its surrounding country was rebuilt with houses and other buildings.

l: Messenian wars, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: is_a wars [between the Messenians and Lacedaemonians] The text describes an early war in which the Lacedaemonians subdued the Messenians after the death of Telecles, a later revolt led by Aristomenes, and a final conflict following a devastating earthquake at Sparta. The Messenians were eventually expelled but later returned when Messene was rebuilt.

l: wall and trench between Cenchreae and Lechaeum, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: is_a fortification [built to block the entrance into Peloponnesus] The Athenians, Lacedaemonians, and their allies constructed a wall and deep trench from Cenchreae to Lechaeum to block the Boeotians from entering the Peloponnesus. Epaminondas identified the Lacedaemonian-held section as weak and broke through it after a fierce assault.

l: Gauls, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Gauls are portrayed chiefly as formidable, often destructive soldiers employed or invading across several conflicts. Sent by Dionysius from Sicily, two thousand aided the Lacedemonians, fought bravely against Boeotians and confederates, received rewards, and returned to Sicily. Under Brennus they invaded Macedonia and Greece to plunder Delphi, but losses, Greek attacks, hunger, cold, and fighting annihilated the army. They served Apollodorus as a cruel life-guard; a garrison left by Pyrrhus plundered Macedonian kings’ sepulchres at Aegae. They offered Perseus aid but departed when payment was refused; Eumenes then subjugated them. They also invaded Italy, defeated Romans at the Allia, captured Rome, and were later routed by Marcus Furius at Trausium.

l: Spaniards, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Spaniards, called alongside Balearic Islanders and others, included two thousand sent with Gauls to aid the Lacedemonians; after courageous service and reward, they returned to Sicily, then came under Asdrubal’s authority and granted him full governmental power.

l: Alexander, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Alexander is a Macedonian king, descended from Hercules on his father’s side and Achilles on his mother’s side. He succeeded Philip, the son of Amyntas, punished Philip’s murderers, secured Macedonia, overcame opposition in Greece, and was recognized as Greece’s general with support for war against Persia. After taking Gaza, he entered Egypt, where cities submitted without fighting; he consulted the oracle of Ammon, which declared him divinely born, and founded Alexandria. He repeatedly led and commanded the Macedonians through long campaigns, persuading them to continue, rewarding and discharging Greek auxiliaries, and extending control through Hyrcania, the Mardian country, Drangina, Arachosia, the Paropamisadae, Bactria, and India. His campaigns brought severe hardship, conquests, submissions, city foundations, and violence: he massacred Massaga mercenaries, subdued Musicanus and Porticanus, and wasted Sambus, while pardoning Brachmanes except leaders of defection. He crossed Caucasus and the Indus, refreshed his army in Taxiles, defeated Porus, restored Porus to his kingdom, and built cities near the river and another Alexandria on the Indus. Wounded but recovered, he sacrificed to the sun, buried Macedonians killed in battle, built ships, and led army and fleet down the Indus. He loved Ptolemy and, through a dream, discovered a healing herb that restored Ptolemy and others. He regarded Hephaestion as a friend with unusually close access, and later arranged Hephaestion’s funeral on an extraordinary scale. Alexander received ambassadors from nearly all parts of the world, then fell severely ill and died after a reign of twelve years and seven months. He gave his ring to Perdiccas and left the kingdom to the most deserving. His death left government without a head and triggered disputes; plans in his notebooks were judged impracticable and set aside.

l: Ismenias, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Ismenias, a close friend of Pelopidas and a man esteemed for his courage, accompanied Pelopidas to Thessaly. Alexander, tyrant of Pherae, seized and imprisoned them both.

l: Pherae, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: has_garrison Cassander's soldiers [Cassander strengthened the garrison] Pherae was ruled by Alexander, who imprisoned Pelopidas and Ismenias and later received opposition from Epaminondas’s forces. The text also identifies Alexander as the tyrant of Pherae.

l: Megalopolis, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Megalopolis is a city built and founded by the Arcadians after defeat by the Lacedemonians, in a secure location and populated from twenty villages. Its forced settlers later left, but Pammenes made them return. Later, supporting Cassander, it withstood Polyperchon’s siege despite damaged towers and walls and an elephant assault.

l: Africa, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Africa contains Carthage and Cyrene with neighbouring cities. It is divided among four kinds of inhabitants: Poeni, Libyan Poeni, Africans, and Numidians. It supplied ten thousand soldiers to the Carthaginian expedition and became the main setting of Agathocles’s war against the Carthaginians. Crossing from Sicily, Agathocles landed with a mixed army in a fertile, wealthy Carthaginian region, captured a great city, moved to Tunis, defeated the Carthaginians, and blockaded Carthage. He gained towns and cities along the coast and in the interior, amid a Numidian revolt, Ophelas’s expedition, and Bomilcar’s coup at Carthage. His advances gave way to recovery by the Carthaginians: his forces were blocked, nearly starved, defeated, and shaken by mutiny and desertion. After his prospects were destroyed, he secretly departed by ship, and peace was made. Later Africa was also the setting for war against mercenaries and Libyans, after which Amilcar was briefly made general of all Libya.

l: Lilybaeum, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Lilybaeum is a Carthaginian city founded after Dionysius ruined Motya. Strongly fortified, sea-supplied, and possessing a harbour, it resisted Pyrrhus and remained Carthaginian; later Romans besieged it and tried to block its harbour, while Carthaginians moved citizens there and repeatedly supplied and defended it.

l: Dionysius the younger, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Dionysius the younger was tyrant and ruler of Syracuse. After Dionysius the tyrant died, he succeeded him, called a senate, sought popular goodwill, held a ceremonial funeral, and secured his throne. He built cities in Apulia to protect shipping and made peace with the Carthaginians, but was portrayed as inactive, slothful, cowardly, and neglectful of military training; his careless war against the Lucanians contributed to losing his dominion. He sent gold-and-ivory statues toward Olympus and Delphi, then sold them for the army after their interception. He regained Syracuse’s Island and castles, but Hicetas took the rest. He surrendered the castle to Timoleon for safe departure to Peloponnesus and died in poor circumstances.

l: Cos, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Cos became populous and prosperous after its people settled there, building a costly large wall and excellent harbor, increasing wealth and revenues; it sent auxiliaries to Byzantium and later received Memnon after Halicarnassus's evacuation.

l: Achaeans, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: The Achaeans side with Tegeans at Mantinea, are a commonwealth in Peloponnesus, and rule Lacedaemon; their assembly hears Roman Senate displeasure, refuses Eumenes’ present, renews their league with Seleucus, and accepts his present.

l: Chares, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Chares was an Athenian general and fleet commander. He replaced Leosthenes and led a fleet against Alexander, frightening enemies but oppressing allies at Corcyra, causing sedition, slaughter, plunder, and harm to Athens’s reputation. During the siege of Chios he commanded land forces, assaulted the walls, and fought the garrison. Sharing fleet command with Iphicrates and Timotheus, he urged battle in a storm, accused them of treason, later gained sole command, and joined Pharnabazus against Persian troops; the Persian king’s complaint helped end the Social War.

l: Laconic and Boeotian War, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: is_a war [between the Lacedaemonians and Boeotians] The Laconic and Boeotian War had continued for more than five years from the Battle of Leuctra. It ended when the Persian king sent ambassadors to persuade the Grecians to agree and set aside their animosities.

l: Battle between the Lacedaemonians and Arcadians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: has_winner Lacedemonians [with no Lacedaemonian losses reported] The battle ended in a decisive victory for the Lacedaemonians, with more than ten thousand Arcadians slain and no Lacedaemonian reported lost. It was the first considerable Lacedaemonian success since the Battle of Leuctra.

l: Epaminondas’s rescue of the Boeotian army, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: is_carried_out_by Epaminondas [while he was a private soldier] During the Boeotian retreat through the plain of Thessaly, Alexander’s cavalry attacked the army’s rear while the troops lacked food and were unable to advance or hold their ground. Although serving as a private soldier, Epaminondas was chosen general, organized the rear guard, repulsed the attackers, and brought the army safely away.

l: Dionysius’s Sicilian war against Carthage, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Dionysius’s war in Sicily against Carthage began with a large attack that took Selinus, Entella, and Eryx, stalled at Lilybaeum, and ended with heavy ship losses at Eryx.

l: Dionysius’s death, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: is_caused_by violent distemper [after excessive drinking at a feast] Dionysius died after ruling for thirty-eight years. He became violently ill after excessive feasting and drinking to celebrate news that his tragedy had won a victory at Athens, a result connected in the text with an oracle that he would die after overcoming those better than himself.

l: Alexander’s massacre at Scotussa, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Alexander, tyrant of Pherae, held a grudge against Scotussa’s inhabitants, summoned them to an assembly, surrounded and killed them, discarded their bodies beyond the walls, and plundered the city.

l: Coos’s fortification and settlement, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: is_a fortification and settlement [of the city of Coos] The people of Coos settled in their later city, increased its population, and enclosed it with a costly large wall. They also provided it with an excellent harbor, after which the city grew in public revenues and private wealth.

l: Arcadian exiles, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Arcadian exiles originate from Elis, raid and seize Lassia in Triphylia, then receive Elean aid during its siege.

l: Triphylia, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: contains Lassia [Lassia is a strong castle] Triphylia was disputed for a long time by the Arcadians and Elians, with possession changing between them. Lassia was identified as a strong castle in Triphylia.

l: Lassia, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Lassia was seized by Arcadian exiles and later besieged by the Arcadians. The Elians fought near it in an unsuccessful attempt to assist the exiles.

l: battle near Lassia, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: The battle near Lassia, between the Elians and Arcadian supporters, ended with the Elians routed after numerical defeat and over two hundred losses.

l: 104th Olympiad, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: The 104th Olympiad was celebrated by Pisates and Arcadians; Phocides of Athens won, while Elians rejected it as forced and unlawful.

l: Pisates, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Pisates claim the traditional right to manage the Olympic games, ally with Arcadians against Elians, defeat them, and manage the games at the 104th Olympiad.

l: dominion of the sea, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Epaminondas urged the Thebans to gain dominion of the sea, arguing that their sovereignty on land would help them become masters at sea. The Thebans decreed the construction of a hundred galleys and docks and sought assistance from Rhodes, Chios, and Byzantium.

l: Theban invasion of Orchomenus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: The Theban invasion of Orchomenus followed the discovery of a conspiracy involving Theban fugitives and three hundred horsemen from Orchomenus. The Thebans captured the city, killed all the men, and sold the women and children as slaves.

l: Pontus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Pontus is a region containing the Cimmerian Bosphorus, with the Temple of the Chalcidonians near its mouth. Eumelus aided Greek inhabitants and protected merchants trading there by fighting the Heniochians, people of Taurus, and Achaians. Later Demetrius occupied and fortified its mouth, leaving infantry and ships; Cassander's forces could not pass the strait.

l: Cyzicum, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: is_a Greek confederate city [a strong peninsula city possessing naval strength] Cyzicum resisted Aridaeus despite being surprised and initially unable to defend itself. Its inhabitants secretly armed the city, obtained help from Byzantium, recovered people trapped outside the walls, and forced Aridaeus to abandon the siege.

l: Xerxes, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: commands the Branchidae [to remove from Miletus] Xerxes commanded the removal of the Branchidae from Miletus when he returned from Greece. The Branchidae were also described as having joined themselves with Xerxes after the violation of the Didymæus temple.

l: Tegeans, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Tegeans lead an Arcadian faction, seek Boeotian aid by ambassador, and fight with Epaminondas and the Boeotian alliance against Mantineans at Mantinea.

l: Cretans, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: The Cretans are a people who serve as couriers for Agis, capture and plunder Siphnos by deception, and are linked by the senate to Cretan pirates. They send ambassadors to Rome, gain then lose favorable judgment, and face demands for ships, hostages, leaders, and silver, causing sedition.

l: battle of Mantinea, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: The battle of Mantinea involved cavalry and infantry on both sides: Mantineans, Lacedaemonians, Elians, Athenians, and allies fought Tegeans, Boeotians, Argives, and confederates. Boeotians routed a Lacedaemonian division, but Epaminondas was mortally wounded. Both sides claimed victory and erected trophies; peace among Arcadians followed, then quickly broke down.

l: general Greek league, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: is_a offensive and defensive league [formed by the Grecians after the battle] After the battle, the war-weary Greeks formed a general offensive and defensive league that included the Messenians. The Lacedaemonians alone refused to swear to its articles because of their hostility toward the Messenians.

l: Orontes, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Orontes, governor of Mysia, joined the Persian revolt and led its army, then betrayed the rebels after receiving soldiers’ pay, seizing messengers and surrendering cities and soldiers.

l: Datames, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Datames, governor of Cappadocia, commanded mercenaries, defeated forces after Mithrobarzanes’s betrayal, and was later killed in an ambush ordered by Artaxerxes.

l: Dion, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Dion is a Syracusan soldier and philosopher, brother of Hipparinus and Megacles and brother-in-law of Dionysius the younger. Suspected by Dionysius because of his noble birth and spirit, he fled Sicily to Peloponnesus and Corinth, then sought help to recover Syracuse's liberty. Sailing from Zacynthus to Minoa with two ships and a thousand mercenaries, he gained Sicilian support, armed Syracusans, and was chosen general with Megacles. He entered Syracuse, fought at the wall, was wounded in the right arm, and helped restore the ancient liberties of the Syracusans and Sicilians. After conflict with the Syracusans, he led foreign soldiers to the Leontines, later rescued Syracuse, and received absolute governorship by unanimous vote. He pardoned his opponents but was ultimately killed by mercenaries of Zacynthus.

l: Leosthenes, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Leosthenes was an Athenian and brave-spirited general. After organizing and paying mercenaries at Tenarus, securing arms, and seeking Aetolian support, he led a Greek confederacy, defeated the Boeotians, and besieged Antipater in Lamia. He died three days after a stone struck his head during a Macedonian sally.

l: Megalopolitans, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: The Megalopolitans were residents of Megalopolis who struggled against the Lacedaemonians, seeking and receiving aid from Argives, Sicyonians, Messenians, and Thebans before making a truce. Later, loyal to Cassander because they favored oligarchy, they prepared fifteen thousand citizens, strangers, and servants for siege, repelled a Macedonian assault, rebuilt defenses, and defeated Polyperchon’s elephants.

l: rebels (Persian revolt), The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: The Persian rebels included coastal peoples, governors, commanders, and allied rulers in Asia. They made Orontes general, but he betrayed them, while Rheomithres later seized revolted lords and officers and sent them to the Persian king.

l: mercenaries (Egyptian campaign), The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Tachos assembled ten thousand Greek mercenaries for his campaign against Persia. Agesilaus received command of them, and they helped him escape the Egyptian siege and defeat the Egyptian army.

l: Asia, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Asia is a region, divided by Mount Taurus into northern and southern parts and described through its provinces, rivers, climates, coastal countries, and inland regions. Its cities on the side within the Halys are specifically noted. Its record unfolds chiefly as a contested and repeatedly reorganized theater of rule and war. Coastal peoples, governors, and commanders revolted against Artaxerxes, depriving the Persian king of half his revenues; Mentor governed the Asiatic shore while Bagoas held the higher parts. Philip sent Attalus and Parmenio toward Asia, and rivalry followed between Macedonian and Persian forces. Alexander entered from Europe across the Hellespont, claimed conquest, campaigned along the coast and inland, and after Issus Asia is described as under a conquering sword; Darius offered him the part within the Halys. Disorder also accompanied these campaigns, as discharged mercenaries robbed the country. After Alexander, Asia was divided among commanders and became the object of struggles involving Eumenes, Antigonus, Cassander, Lysimachus, Demetrius, Seleucus, and others. Antigonus sought its provinces, became its undisputed absolute lord, and used beacons and couriers to manage it, though later warfare again spread through its cities and regions. Asia also saw a slave uprising and harsh government under Attalus. Under Roman administration it suffered illegal exactions by publicans, then relief under Quintus Mutius Scaevola; afterward Mithridates's party drove cities to revolt from the Romans. Following Antiochus's overthrow, Roman commissioners redistributed territories in Asia among Eumenes, the Rhodians, and freed cities.

l: Pisidia, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Pisidia was the site of Antigonus’s campaign against Alcetas. After Alcetas’s defeat and death, Antigonus left the region, while young men of Termessus continued raiding territory associated with Antigonus.

l: Phoenicia, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Phoenicia, containing Tyre, is a region of cities whose coastal position, ships, grain, timber, and closeness to Egypt made it a repeated prize in war. It revolted from Persian control, with Sidon as the chief resistance center, but was recovered after Artaxerxes marched against it. When Alexander entered, its other cities submitted, while Tyre alone resisted. Later Ptolemy occupied its cities with garrisons; Eumenes sought ships there; and Antigonus built a fleet through its rulers, coastal arsenals, and wood from Mount Libanus. After Ptolemy destroyed or abandoned the principal cities he held, Antigonus recovered Phoenicia without a blow.

l: Cappadocia, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Cappadocia is a kingdom and region, claimed through its royal genealogy to descend from Cyrus. After Ariarathes’ defeat, Perdiccas conquered it and assigned its government to Eumenes of Cardia. It became a central site of Eumenes’ struggles: he defeated Craterus and Neoptolemus there, was later defeated by Antigonus and fled to Nora, briefly returned after his release, and left again as Menander approached. Antigonus also marched from Cappadocia against Alcetas. Later, Eumenes’ killing of Ariarathes brought it under Macedonian control, but Ariarathes’ adopted heir recovered it with Armenian aid. Under a later Ariarathes, it welcomed learned Greeks and renewed friendship with the Romans.

l: Persian revolt, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: The Persian revolt spread among coastal peoples, provincial governors, and commanders who opposed Artaxerxes. Its leaders suffered repeated betrayals by Orontes and Rheomithres, weakening the rebellion and restoring Persian control over several cities and forces.

l: war between Persia and Egypt, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: The war began when Tachos declared war against Persia and prepared ships and troops with Lacedaemonian and Greek support. Tachos later fled to Artaxerxes after Nectanabis seized Egypt, and Artaxerxes made him general against the Egyptians.

l: restoration of Tachos, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Tachos was restored to Egypt after Agesilaus led his forces through the Egyptian encirclement and defeated Nectanabis's army in ground protected by water. Tachos rewarded Agesilaus with honorable gifts before dismissing him.

l: Agesilaus's victory over the Egyptians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Agesilaus defeated the Egyptians after choosing a position secured on both sides by water from the river. The Egyptian numbers gave them little advantage there, and their army was slaughtered and put to flight.

l: Megalopolitan civic conflict, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: The Megalopolitan civic conflict arose when neighboring towns returned from Megalopolis to their former settlements after the peace following Mantinea. Athens sent Pammenes, who forced the towns to return and ended the disturbance.

l: Chares's abuses in Corcyra, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Chares caused seditions and tumults in Corcyra, an allied city. His actions produced slaughter, plunder, and confiscation of property and caused the Athenians to be condemned by their allies.

l: Egyptian fleet, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Tachos prepared an Egyptian fleet of two hundred ships for the war against Persia. Chabrias was appointed its admiral, serving Tachos privately rather than under public authority.

l: Alexander, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Alexander is a Macedonian king, son of Philip and Olympias, descended from Hercules and Achilles, whose career is defined by command, conquest, and the overthrow of Persia. After securing his authority by suppressing revolts and destroying Thebes, he seeks quiet in Greece so that he can invade Asia. He crosses into Asia, claims it with a spear cast ashore, wins at Granicus, Issus, and Arbela, and takes or subdues cities and regions including Miletus, Caria, Tyre, Gaza, Babylon, Persepolis, Sogdiana, and territories toward India. His campaigns depend on personal courage, siegecraft, army organization, and repeated direct leadership, but bring wounds, hardship, mutinies, and resistance. His rule combines severity with generosity and clemency. He honors and supports Darius's family, restores Ada, aids maimed Greek captives, grants liberty to Nysa, rewards soldiers, and treats Persian prisoners civilly; he also plunders Persepolis, destroys cities, executes mutiny leaders, and kills Clitus in drunken rage, then mourns and condemns himself for it. He increasingly joins Macedonian and Persian interests through Persian appointments, Persian bodyguards, mass marriages, his marriage to Statira, and his trust in Persians, provoking Macedonian opposition. He is also married to Roxana, whom he loves. After reaching India and surviving severe danger and exhaustion, he returns through Gedrosia, reaches Susa and then Babylon, and orders Greek exiles recalled shortly before his death. He dies at Babylon, leaving no child to succeed him according to one record, though other records name a son. His body is carried toward Egypt and honored there. His legacy is the ruined Persian empire, cities called Alexandria, and enduring memory of extraordinary deeds, kindnesses, ambition, and power.

l: Macedonians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: The Macedonians are a people repeatedly shown as the core soldiers and army of Macedonia, first restored by Philip after a disastrous defeat by the Illyrians. Philip rebuilds their confidence through speeches, training, and close formation, then leads them to victories over Athenians, Paeones, Illyrians, and allied Thracian powers, raising the kingdom’s wealth, majesty, and glory. Under Alexander they become an expansive campaigning force: they capture Thebes, cross into Asia in large numbers, defeat Persian forces at the Granicus and Issus, seize cities and treasures, build the broad mole and take Tyre, cross the Tigris, and defeat the Persians despite fear, wounds, and casualties. Their campaigns include plundering Persepolis, burning its palace, hard marches through snow and India, assaults on forts and cities, and difficult operations using sarissas, crampirons, cords, and signals. They are recognized for hardiness and valor, but also commit killings, enslavement, and plunder. Their relationship with Alexander is central but unstable. They at times follow him through extreme hazards, rejoice at successes, and receive rewards; at other times they want to return home, reject his plans, refuse to cross the Ganges, object to Persian appointments, and resist divine honors for him. After his death, they become a decisive military and political body: they support or abandon rival commanders and rulers, choose protectors, mutiny, condemn enemies, favor Polyperchon, shift between Eurydice, Olympias, Cassander, Antigonus, and Eumenes, and ultimately betray Eumenes after suffering the loss of their families and baggage. Their later history ends in defeat by Paulus Æmilius and the Romans, followed by liberation and reduced tribute from the Roman Senate; Macedonians in Rome are then ordered to leave Italy after war is declared against Perseus.

l: Paeones, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: The Pæones raided Macedon while it was weakened by war and threatened another invasion. After Philip made a temporary peace with them, he invaded following the death of their king Agis, defeated them, and brought them under Macedonian rule.

l: Thracians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: The Thracians are a people of Thrace who possessed territory, forts, and castles. Allied with Scythians against Lysimachus, they captured Agathocles and returned him with gifts seeking protection and restoration. Their soldiers spared Lysimachus for the public good. Later they suffered Diegylis’s brutality, and nobles fled to Attalus.

l: Amphictyons, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: The Amphictyons are a religious and political court with an Amphictyonic senate or council. They issue decrees, condemn the Phocians and Lacedaemonians to fines, and order Phocian land confiscated and devoted to the deity if payment fails; the Greek approval of this decree prompts Phocian resistance. They then decree war on the Phocians for sacrilege and violation of Apollo's temple treasures, while threatening death for mercenaries who aid them. After Phocian surrender, the council imposes penalties and restores the oracle and religious peace. Later, at Pylene, it agrees to make Alexander generalissimo of Greece.

l: Amphipolis, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Amphipolis was the principal object of Athenian concern in the conflict with Philip. Philip secured peace with Athens by agreeing to abandon all his claim to the city. Amphipolis was attacked and captured by Philip after he was provoked by its injuries. Philip battered its walls, entered through the ruins, killed many opponents, executed his chief enemies, and spared the rest.

l: Methone, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Methone was besieged and captured by Philip of Macedon after Philip learned that its citizens intended to surrender it to his enemies. Its inhabitants were allowed to leave with their clothes, and Philip razed the city and divided its territory among the Macedonians.

l: Cremides, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Philip marched to Cremides, enlarged it, and increased its population.

l: Philippi, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Philip renamed the enlarged city of Cremides Philippi. He also developed the nearby gold mines, which produced a yearly revenue of more than a thousand talents.

l: Cyrene, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: Cyrene, a city in Cyrenaica, resists Thimbron amid internal conflict and bread shortage; after Ophelas defeats him, it is placed under Ptolemy, while Ophelas controls it and neighboring cities and receives Agathocles' request for aid.

l: Philip’s reign in Macedon, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
s: lasts two-and-thirty years Philip reigned as king of Macedon for thirty-two years. He transformed Macedon from a kingdom subject to the Illyrians into the greatest kingdom in Europe and established authority over many cities and countries.

l: the Illyrian invasion of Macedon, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian
